etymology: From Latin obdurare, to harden against: a heart made stubborn toward reproof. Webster 1828 names it invincible hardness of heart, impenitence that cannot be subdued, and obstinacy in wickedness.
biblical_def: Obduracy is a heart hardened against the word of God until it will not hear. They made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and great wrath came from the LORD of hosts (Zec 7:12). After hardness and an impenitent heart, a man treasures up wrath against the day of wrath (Rom 2:5). The danger is not a hard day. It is a settled refusal to be corrected, and the church is charged to exhort one another daily lest any be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OB'DURACY as invincible hardness of heart; impenitence that cannot be subdued; inflexible persistency in sin; obstinacy in wickedness.
webster_full: OB'DURACY, noun — Invincible hardness of heart; impenitence that cannot be subdued; inflexible persistency in sin; obstinacy in wickedness.
God may by almighty grace hinder the absolute completion of sin in final obduracy.
scriptures: Zechariah 7:12

Yea, they made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts.
Romans 2:5
But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God;
corruption_summary: The age renames obduracy as strength of will, boundaries, or a man who will not be shamed into change.
corruption_paragraphs: A heart that will not hear the law is now often praised as independence. Scripture calls it adamant. Wrath follows the refusal, not because God is petty, but because He has spoken and been despised.
Final obduracy is not a mood that passes with rest. It is impenitence that will not be subdued. The remedy is not a softer vocabulary. It is daily exhortation, and grace that breaks the stone.
roots_summary: Latin ob and durus name a heart hardened against. The KJV speaks of a hard heart, an impenitent heart, and being hardened through deceit. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin obdurare — to harden against correction.
KJV adamant stone is the picture of a people who will not hear the law (Zec 7:12).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun obduracy.
usage: Obduracy is invincible hardness of heart, not admirable resolve.
Do not treasure up wrath by refusing correction.
Exhort one another daily, lest sin harden the heart.

etymology: From Latin pusillus, very small, and animus, mind or courage: a small soul. Webster 1828 defines it as want of the firmness that constitutes courage, and a feebleness that shrinks from trifling or imaginary dangers.
biblical_def: Pusillanimity is smallness of soul, the spirit of fear that God does not give. God hath not given us the spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind (2 Tim 1:7). The fearful stand with the unbelieving in the lake of fire (Rev 21:8). In Israel the fainthearted were sent home, lest their fear make their brethren's heart faint also (Deu 20:8). This is not the fear of the LORD, which is wisdom. It is shrinking from the duty God has assigned.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PUSILLANIM'ITY as want of that firmness and strength of mind which constitutes courage or fortitude; weakness of spirit; cowardliness; that feebleness of mind which shrinks from trifling or imaginary dangers.
webster_full: PUSILLANIM'ITY, noun [Latin pusillanimitas; pusillus, small, weak, and animus, courage.] Want of that firmness and strength of mind which constitutes courage or fortitude; weakness of spirit; cowardliness; that feebleness of mind which shrinks from trifling or imaginary dangers.
It is obvious to distinguish between an act of pusillanimity and an act of great modesty or humility.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 1:7
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
Revelation 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
corruption_summary: Modern speech baptizes pusillanimity as sensitivity, caution, or mental health, and calls courage toxic.
corruption_paragraphs: A small soul that shrinks from a real duty is not thereby gentle. Webster already distinguished pusillanimity from modesty and humility. Scripture distinguishes the spirit of fear from power, love, and a sound mind.
The other error mocks every fear, including the fear of the LORD. Pusillanimity is not reverence. It is feebleness that will not stand when God has spoken, and it can make a brother's heart faint.
roots_summary: Latin pusillanimitas is smallness of spirit. The KJV speaks of the spirit of fear, the fearful, and the fainthearted. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin pusillus and animus — a small soul; want of courage.
KJV spirit of fear is denied as God's gift to the church (2 Tim 1:7).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun pusillanimity.
usage: Pusillanimity is weakness of spirit, not humility.
God has not given His people the spirit of fear.
Do not let a faintheart make the brethren faint.

etymology: From Latin rapacitas, from rapax and rapio, to seize. Webster 1828 gives addictedness to plunder, the practice of seizing by force, and extorting by oppressive injustice.
biblical_def: Rapacity is the habit of seizing what belongs to another. They covet fields and take them by violence, and houses, and oppress a man and his heritage (Mic 2:2). The ways of everyone greedy of gain take away the life of the owners thereof (Prov 1:19). Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high (Hab 2:9). The sin is not enterprise. It is plunder dressed as gain, and oppression dressed as success.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RAPAC'ITY as addictedness to plunder; the act or practice of seizing by force; and the act or practice of extorting or exacting by oppressive injustice.
webster_full: RAPAC'ITY, noun [Latin rapacitas, from rapax, rapio.]

1. Addictedness to plunder; the exercise of plunder; the act or practice of seizing by force; as the rapacity of a conquering army; the rapacity of pirates; the rapacity of a Turkish pashaw; the rapacity of extortioners.
2. Ravenousness; as the rapacity of animals.
3. The act or practice of extorting or exacting by oppressive injustice.
scriptures: Micah 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
Proverbs 1:19
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.
corruption_summary: Rapacity is rebranded as hustle, market discipline, or a winner's appetite, so long as the seizure is legal enough.
corruption_paragraphs: A conquering appetite for other men's fields does not become virtue because it files papers. Micah names the coveting and the violence together. Proverbs says the greedy way takes life, not merely margin.
Webster's third sense is exacting by oppressive injustice. Interest, rent, and office can all wear that face. The dictionary will not call plunder prudence.
roots_summary: Latin rapio is to seize. The KJV speaks of taking by violence, greed of gain, and evil covetousness. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin rapacitas — addictedness to seizing by force.
KJV take them by violence joins coveting to oppression (Mic 2:2).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun rapacity.
usage: Rapacity is the practice of seizing by force, not sharp business.
Do not covet a man's field and call the taking success.
Greed of gain takes away the life of its owners.

etymology: From Latin profligare, to dash down, ruin, or cast away. Webster 1828 defines profligacy as a very vicious course of life, a state of being abandoned in moral principle and in vice.
biblical_def: Profligacy is a life given over to vice, past feeling. They have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness (Eph 4:19). The time past may suffice to have walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, and abominable idolatries (1 Pet 4:3). She that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth (1 Tim 5:6). The word is not a slur on joy. It is the name for a course abandoned to lust and waste.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROF'LIGACY as a profligate or very vicious course of life; a state of being abandoned in moral principle and in vice.
webster_full: PROF'LIGACY, noun — A profligate or very vicious course of life; a state of being abandoned in moral principle and in vice.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:19
Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.
1 Peter 4:3
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
corruption_summary: Profligacy is sold as liberation, a season of finding oneself, or the ordinary recreation of successful men.
corruption_paragraphs: A course abandoned in moral principle is not a personality. Scripture says such men are past feeling, and that the time past ought to suffice. Pleasure that lives while the soul is dead is not health.
The church is not called to envy the riot and then baptize it as authenticity. The old word still fits: vicious course, principle cast away, vice as a settled life.
roots_summary: Latin profligatus is one dashed down and abandoned. The KJV speaks of lasciviousness, uncleanness, and living in pleasure. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin profligare — to cast down; a life ruined by vice.
KJV given themselves over unto lasciviousness is the picture of abandonment (Eph 4:19).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun profligacy.
usage: Profligacy is a vicious course of life, not a colorful youth.
The time past in lust and excess ought to suffice.
Do not call a life past feeling freedom.

etymology: From Latin duplicitas, doubleness. Webster 1828 keeps the moral sense: doubleness of heart or speech, dissembling one's real opinions to conceal them and mislead, double-dealing, dissimulation, deceit.
biblical_def: Duplicity is a double heart. They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak (Ps 12:2). The integrity of the upright guides them, but the perverseness of transgressors destroys them (Prov 11:3). James commands sinners to cleanse their hands and the double minded to purify their hearts (Jas 4:8). Two speeches about the same thing, fitted to the hearer, are not wisdom. They are deceit.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines duplicity, in its moral sense, as doubleness of heart or speech; dissembling one's real opinions to conceal them and mislead; double-dealing; dissimulation; deceit.
webster_full: DUPLICITY, noun [Latin, double.]
1. Doubleness; the number two.

2. Doubleness of heart or speech; the act or practice of exhibiting a different or contrary conduct, or uttering different or contrary sentiments, at different times, in relation to the same thing; or the act of dissembling ones real opinions for the purpose of concealing them and misleading persons in the conversation and intercourse of life; double-dealing; dissimulation; deceit.
3. In law, duplicity is the pleading of two or more distinct matters or single pleas.
scriptures: Psalm 12:2
They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak.
James 4:8
Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.
corruption_summary: Duplicity is praised as messaging, diplomacy, or reading the room, so long as the two speeches are smooth.
corruption_paragraphs: A man who utters contrary sentiments about the same thing, to different hearers, is not skilled. He is double. Flattering lips and a double heart are the psalm's pair, and both are vanity.
The law sense, pleading two matters as one, has its own place. The moral sense does not. God draws nigh to the purified heart, not to the managed one.
roots_summary: Latin duplex is twofold. The KJV speaks of a double heart and the double minded. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin duplicitas — doubleness of heart or speech.
KJV double heart stands with flattering lips (Ps 12:2).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun duplicity.
usage: Duplicity is doubleness of heart, not tact.
Do not speak one thing to one man and the contrary to another.
Purify the double mind; do not manage it.

etymology: From Latin credulitas, from credo, to believe. Webster 1828 defines it as easiness of belief: assent without sufficient evidence, a disposition to believe on slight evidence or none at all.
biblical_def: Credulity is belief without trial. The simple believeth every word, but the prudent man looketh well to his going (Prov 14:15). Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God, because many false prophets are gone out into the world (1 Jn 4:1). For this cause God shall send strong delusion, that they should believe a lie (2 Thess 2:11). Faith rests on God's word. Credulity rests on the last voice that sounded confident.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CREDULITY as easiness of belief; a weakness of mind by which a person yields assent without sufficient evidence; a disposition to believe on slight evidence or no evidence at all.
webster_full: CREDULITY, noun [Latin, to believe.] Easiness of belief; a weakness of mind by which a person is disposed to believe, or yield his assent to a declaration or proposition, without sufficient evidence of the truth of what is said or proposed; a disposition to believe on slight evidence or no evidence at all.
scriptures: Proverbs 14:15
The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
1 John 4:1
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: The age calls credulity open-mindedness when the tale flatters, and calls tested faith closed-minded.
corruption_paragraphs: To believe every word is not charity. It is simplicity in the bad sense, and false prophets depend on it. Scripture commands a trial of spirits, not a shrug.

The opposite theft treats all belief as credulity, including faith in what God has said. Webster's word is assent without evidence. The gospel is not that. It is a word attested, to be believed, and not every competing spirit with it.
roots_summary: Latin credulus is ready to believe. The KJV contrasts the simple who believes every word with the command to try the spirits. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin credo — to believe; here, belief too lightly given.
KJV believeth every word marks the simple, not the prudent (Prov 14:15).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun credulity.
usage: Credulity believes on slight evidence or none.
Do not believe every spirit; try them.
Faith in God's word is not the same as believing every word.

etymology: From Latin incredulitas, the quality of not believing. Webster 1828 defines it as indisposition to believe, a withholding or refusal of belief, and names religious unbelief the most irrational kind.
biblical_def: Incredulity is refusal to believe what God has shown. Thomas was told, Be not faithless, but believing (Jn 20:27). Take heed lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God (Heb 3:12). A wise man feareth and departeth from evil, but the fool rageth and is confident (Prov 14:16). The vice is not caution about rumors. It is a settled indisposition to credit God, often proud of itself.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines INCREDU'LITY as the quality of not believing; indisposition to believe; a withholding or refusal of belief.
webster_full: INCREDU'LITY, noun The quality of not believing; indisposition to believe; a withholding or refusal of belief.
Of every species of incredulity, religious unbelief is infinitely the most irrational.
scriptures: John 20:27
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
Hebrews 3:12
Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God.
corruption_summary: Incredulity toward God is treated as the default of intelligent men, while incredulity toward the age's own tales is treated as vice.
corruption_paragraphs: Refusal to believe is not automatically honesty. An evil heart of unbelief departs from the living God. Webster called religious unbelief the most irrational species of the vice, because it withholds credit where the evidence is God's own word and work.
Christ did not flatter Thomas's delay. He showed His wounds and commanded belief. Caution about liars remains a duty. Incredulity toward the risen Lord is another thing, and it is sin.
roots_summary: Latin in and credulus name the refusal to believe. The KJV speaks of faithless and of an evil heart of unbelief. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin incredulitas — withholding or refusal of belief.
KJV be not faithless, but believing answers the doubt of Thomas (Jn 20:27).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun incredulity.
usage: Incredulity is refusal of belief, not automatic wisdom.
Be not faithless, but believing.
An evil heart of unbelief departs from the living God.

etymology: From Latin infidelitas, want of faith or faithfulness. Webster 1828 gives want of belief, disbelief of the Scriptures, unfaithfulness in marriage, and breach of trust.
biblical_def: Infidelity is want of faith, and want of faithfulness. Unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; even their mind and conscience is defiled (Tit 1:15). Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge (Heb 13:4). The LORD has been witness against the man who dealt treacherously with the wife of his youth, the wife of his covenant (Mal 2:14). Unbelief and adultery are not the same act. Both break faith: one with God, one with the covenant of the bed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines INFIDEL'ITY as want of faith or belief; disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures; unfaithfulness in marriage; and breach of trust.
webster_full: INFIDEL'ITY, noun [Latin infidelitas.]
1. In general, want of faith or belief; a withholding of credit.
2. Disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine original of christianity; unbelief.
3. Unfaithfulness, particularly in married persons; a violation of the marriage covenant by adultery or lewdness.
4. Breach of trust; treachery; deceit; as the infidelity of a friend or a servant. In this sense, unfaithfulness is most used.
scriptures: Titus 1:15
Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled.
Hebrews 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: Infidelity in marriage is softened to an affair or a need, and infidelity toward Scripture is treated as sophistication.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster kept both senses, and both are still sins. Disbelief of the divine original of Christianity is not a neutral method. A defiled conscience calls impure what God calls pure, and calls pure what God will judge.
The marriage sense is not a private arrangement between adults. It is treachery against the wife of the covenant, and the LORD is witness. Do not rename adultery as growth.
roots_summary: Latin infidelitas is want of faith and of faithfulness. The KJV speaks of the unbelieving and of adulterers whom God will judge. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin infidelitas — want of belief, or breach of faith.
KJV unbelieving marks a defiled mind and conscience (Tit 1:15).
KJV adulterers names the violation of the marriage bed (Heb 13:4).
usage: Infidelity is want of faith, and unfaithfulness to a covenant.
Do not treat disbelief of Scripture as a mark of a clean mind.
God will judge the violation of the marriage bed.
